newsitem.title: USA: Libertarian, Lefty square off in Texas campaign.
newsitem.headline: Libertarian, Lefty square off in Texas campaign.

text.p: In a Texas campaign considered pivotal for Republicans fighting to maintain a majority in Congress, a former Libertarian who advocates the legalization of drugs is battling it out against a right-leaning Lefty.

Republican Ron Paul and Democrat Charles "Lefty" Morris are locked in a mud-slinging, down-and-dirty race to replace incumbent Greg Laughlin, a former Democrat who switched parties only to be ousted by Paul in last spring's Republican primary.
Polls conducted by both parties show a very tight race for the seat in a district that stretches from the coastal lowlands southwest of Houston to the hill country near Austin in central Texas.

Battling for votes in a conservative district, Morris raced to the right of his Republican opponent on the drug issue, calling for more border patrols and an FBI office in Victoria, a byway for drugs flowing across the U.S.-Mexico border to Houston.

"(District voters) don't want a member of Congress who has been going around the country for the last 10 years giving speeches advocating the legalization of drugs," said Billy Rogers, Morris' campaign manager.

Paul fired back by criticizing Morris, a San Marcos lawyer, for accepting the bulk of his estimated $1 million in campaign funding from trial lawyers. The AFL-CIO, meanwhile, weighed in with attack ads on local television featuring a Paul speech advocating legalization of drugs.
"(Morris) is owned by trial lawyers and the labor unions. In this district if I do my job and get that message out, he can't win," said Paul, who expects to raise $750,000 to bankroll his campaign.

Paul has been endorsed by House Majority Whip Tom DeLay, a Republican from the neighboring 22nd Congressional District, and baseball legend Nolan Ryan, who hails from nearby Alvin and pitched in as honorary campaign chairman.

The key to the campaign, pundits said, is whether voters can overlook Paul's controversial stands advocating the legalization of drugs and defending cross-burning as a form of free speech protected by the Constitution.

"He's always been a quirky Libertarian on thing like public education and drugs," said University of Houston political scientist Richard Murray. "(But) he fuzzes that up when he's running for Congress in a race like this."

Paul, a Surfside gynecologist who served in Congress from 1976 to 1984 before making a failed bid for U.S. Senate, said he is not racist and his stand on cross-burning as a form of free speech was taken out of context.

"Cross burning could be a crime if they were violating somebody's property rights. But if you go out in your farm someplace and it's on your property and you put two sticks together and you burn it, I am not going to send in the federal police," he said.
